This study introduces a novel methodology, denoted as mmf, designed to automate the process of segmenting cosmic structure into its fundamental constituents, namely clusters, filaments, and walls. A distinguishing feature of this approach is its inherent scale independence, thereby enabling the identification of all structural entities irrespective of their size or morphological characteristics. As such, the method is particularly well-suited for extracting comprehensive catalogues of clusters, walls, and filaments from galaxy samples within redshift surveys or from particle distributions in cosmological n-body simulations. Notably, mmf does not rely on any prior assumptions regarding the scale or shape of the structures, thereby facilitating an unbiased analysis of cosmic structure formation and evolution. The development of this method has significant implications for our understanding of large-scale structure, enabling researchers to systematically investigate the properties and relationships between various structural components in a manner that is both efficient and accurate.

This study employs resistive magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) nested grid simulations to investigate the driving mechanism of jets and outflows in the star formation process. The numerical model calculates cloud evolution from the molecular cloud core to the stellar core, revealing two distinct flow regimes within the collapsing cloud core. Low-velocity flows (~5 km/s) with a wide opening angle are driven by the adiabatic core, while high-velocity flows (~30 km/s) with good collimation originate from the protostar. The degree of collimation between these flows is attributed to variations in magnetic field strength and configuration. Specifically, strong hourglass-like magnetic fields surrounding the adiabatic core facilitate magnetocentrifugal acceleration, whereas weak straight-field lines around the protostar drive flow via magnetic pressure gradient forces. Differing gravitational potential depths between the adiabatic core and protostar also contribute to variations in flow speed. The results suggest that low-velocity flows correspond to observed molecular outflows, while high-velocity flows are associated with optical jets, implying that these phenomena are driven by distinct cores rather than being entrained by one another.

This treatise presents a comprehensive generalization of the standard gluing theorem for index 1 pseudoholomorphic curves within the context of contact manifold symplectization. Specifically, it is demonstrated that when considering two such curves, u_+ and u_-, with embedded Reeb orbits gamma, the total multiplicity of negative ends of u_+ at covers of gamma can be reconciled with the total multiplicity of positive ends of u_- at covers of gamma, even in scenarios where individual multiplicities diverge. The proposed gluing method involves inserting genus zero branched covers of r-invariant cylinders between u_+ and u_-, resulting in an index 2 curve. Notably, the signed count of such gluings is shown to be equivalent to a signed count of zeroes of a specific section of an obstruction bundle over the moduli space of branched covers of the cylinder. This result, which builds upon the combinatorial formula derived in Part I, has significant implications for the differential d in embedded contact homology, where it is established that d^2=0. Furthermore, the presented gluing technique is extensible to a broader range of problems, and supplementary lemmas regarding the generic behavior of pseudoholomorphic curves in symplectizations are also provided.

This study presents an investigation into the analogue model of cosmological particle creation within a Friedmann-Robertson-Walker universe, utilizing numerical simulations of a Bose-Einstein condensate with a time-dependent scattering length. Specifically, a two-dimensional homogeneous condensate is examined via the classical field method, employing the truncated Wigner approximation. The results demonstrate that for various forms of the scaling function, particle production is consistent with theoretical expectations in the long wavelength limit. This finding has significant implications for our understanding of the underlying theory, particularly in relation to modified dispersion relations arising from the microscopic theory of a weakly interacting Bose gas. Furthermore, this research provides insight into the possibility of investigating phenomena not readily accessible in their cosmological counterparts through analogue models of gravity. The numerical simulations presented herein provide a novel approach to exploring the complex dynamics of particle creation in these systems, shedding light on the intricate relationships between micro- and macroscopic scales.

This study undertakes an in-depth examination of the abelianization process for the symmetric mapping class group of a double unbranched cover, with particular emphasis on its relationship to the Riemann theta constant, Schottky theta constant, and the theta multiplier. Through a rigorous application of these mathematical constructs, the researcher establishes a comprehensive framework for determining the abelianization of this group, thereby providing valuable insights into its underlying structure. Furthermore, the investigation extends to the derivation of lower bounds for the abelianizations of certain finite index subgroups of the mapping class group, thus contributing to a more nuanced understanding of the subgroup's properties and behavior. The research methodology employed is grounded in established mathematical theories, with the results demonstrating a significant advancement in the field of geometric topology and algebraic geometry. The findings have far-reaching implications for ongoing research initiatives and are expected to stimulate further inquiry into the abelianization process and its applications.

This study undertakes a comprehensive examination of the hyperfine coupling constant's behavior for a phosphorus donor in silicon, situated below the ionization regime and in proximity to interfaces. Utilizing both tight-binding and band minima basis approaches, the research team has conducted electronic structure calculations involving over 3 million atoms, thereby providing a highly detailed understanding of the system's properties. Notably, the results obtained from these theoretical frameworks demonstrate a striking agreement with recent precision measurements, particularly with regard to the quadratic Stark coefficient. This convergence between theory and experiment represents a significant advancement in the field, underscoring the accuracy of these approaches for predicting single donor spin control behavior. Furthermore, the study reveals that the presence of interfaces gives rise to a pronounced linear Stark effect, whereas the quadratic effect dominates at greater distances from the interface. The findings of this research have far-reaching implications for the development of quantum computing applications, where precise control over single donor spin states is essential.

This research presents an extension of the mean-field theory for the spinless Bose-Hubbard model to encompass the diverse superfluid phases that emerge in the spin-1 case. By developing a comprehensive mean-field framework, it is possible to distinguish between polar and ferromagnetic superfluids, as well as Mott insulators that arise at integer fillings at zero temperature, and normal Bose liquids into which these Mott insulators transition at finite temperatures. Notably, the study reveals that several of the superfluid-Mott insulator transitions exhibit first-order behavior at finite temperatures, in contrast to the spinless case. The resulting phase diagrams are characterized by a rich interplay between first- and second-order transitions, as well as tricritical points. This work provides a fundamental understanding of the complex phase behavior in the spin-1 Bose-Hubbard model and offers insights into the possibility of realizing such phase diagrams in experimental systems, thereby facilitating further research into the underlying physics.

This study presents a rigorous proof of the vector identity proposed by Gubarev, Stodolsky, and Zakarov, which establishes a fundamental relationship between the volume integral of the square of a 3-vector field and non-local integrals involving its curl and divergence. The mathematical framework underlying this identity is carefully examined, with particular attention paid to the derivation of the relevant expressions. Subsequently, the proposed identity is applied to a specific case study, namely the magnetic vector potential and magnetic field generated by a rotating charged shell. This application serves as a paradigmatic example of the utility of the Gubarev-Stodolsky-Zakarov (GSZ) identity in the context of electromagnetic theory. Furthermore, the analysis involves a straightforward exercise in the use of the addition theorem of spherical harmonics, thereby underscoring the importance of this mathematical tool in the solution of problems involving rotational symmetry. The proof and application presented herein provide a comprehensive examination of the GSZ identity, shedding light on its theoretical foundations and practical applications.

This study investigates the plasma effects within a micromachined high-electron mobility transistor (HEMT) utilizing a microcantilever as the gate, wherein a developed model is employed to account for both mechanical motion of the microcantilever and spatio-temporal variations in the two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) system. The model incorporates a point-mass approximation to describe the microcantilever's mechanical motion, while the hydrodynamic electron transport model is utilized to elucidate distributed electron plasma phenomena within the 2DEG system. Through application of this model, calculations were performed to determine the response function characterizing the amplitude of microcantilever oscillations and output electric signal as functions of signal frequency and bias voltage for devices with varying parameters. The results indicate that the frequency of mechanical resonance and its damping exhibit distinct voltage dependences, with pronounced maxima in the amplitudes of both mechanical oscillations and output electric signals observed at bias voltages proximal to the 2DEG channel depletion threshold, followed by a precipitous decline with further increases in bias voltage.

This paper presents an investigation into the relationship between the cosmological scale factor and scalar field within the framework of Wheeler-DeWitt equation. By leveraging this connection, the authors derive a tunnel effect for the cosmological scale factor, as well as a quantum potential well associated with the scalar field. These findings are subsequently integrated into the physics of cosmic quantum birth, thereby providing a novel solution to the Wheeler-DeWitt equation. The resultant general probability distribution of cosmic birth is derived through this analysis, enabling a comprehensive examination of the underlying cosmological processes. The authors' approach facilitates a deeper understanding of the quantum origins of the universe, shedding light on the fundamental mechanisms governing cosmic evolution. By reconciling the Wheeler-DeWitt equation with the principles of quantum mechanics, this research contributes significantly to our comprehension of the early stages of the cosmos, thereby advancing the field of cosmological quantum theory.

This study examines the integration of radar and remote sensing technologies into intelligent transportation systems (ITS) with the aim of mitigating road accidents worldwide. Statistical analysis indicates that the incorporation of wireless radar systems in vehicles could potentially reduce annual road fatalities by 8-10%. To effectively implement such a system, it is essential to select a suitable wireless technology capable of navigating severe interference present on open roads. A combined digital approach incorporating spread spectrum and diversity reception techniques is proposed as a viable solution. Specifically, the study advocates for the adoption of Frequency Hopping Spread Spectrum (FHSS) based space diversity systems operating within the 5.8 GHz Industrial Scientific and Medical (ISM) band with an available bandwidth of 80 MHz. This choice offers the added benefit of unlicensed operation. The system's radio channel is characterized to inform efficient design, with a focus on radar mode, which enables conditional measurement of the nearest vehicle's range following authentication of received codes. To facilitate simultaneous communication and radar functionality, a software-defined radio approach has been initiated, prioritizing speed and flexibility in system implementation.

This abstract presents an examination of recent advancements in broadband wireless technology, specifically CDMA and UWB systems, which have facilitated significant development efforts in wireless communication and imaging radar systems. The convergence of communication and radar technologies is also being pursued, with potential applications in Intelligent Transport Systems (ITS) and other areas. This trend has motivated the present authors to investigate the integration of communication technologies with radar capabilities, utilizing DS-UWB wireless technology to achieve interference-free and clutter-free remote imaging of targets. By leveraging the synergies between these disciplines, researchers aim to enhance the quality and accuracy of remote sensing applications, ultimately contributing to the advancement of ITS and related fields. The development of such convergence technologies is well-justified by the rapid growth of broadband wireless technology, which has created new opportunities for innovation and collaboration across traditional boundaries.

This manuscript presents a rigorous derivation of Mirzakhani's recursive formula for the Weil-Petersson volumes of moduli spaces of curves, leveraging the Witten-Kontsevich theorem as a fundamental tool. The authors' proof provides a novel and elegant solution to this long-standing problem in algebraic geometry, thereby contributing significantly to our understanding of the intricate relationships between these mathematical structures. Furthermore, the manuscript delves into the properties of intersection numbers involving higher degree κ-classes, shedding light on their behavior within the context of moduli spaces. By harnessing the power of the Witten-Kontsevich theorem, the authors demonstrate a profound connection between topological invariants and geometric quantities, thereby illuminating the rich tapestry of mathematical relationships that govern these complex systems. This work not only serves as a testament to the enduring influence of Mirzakhani's pioneering research but also opens up new avenues for exploration at the intersection of algebraic geometry, topology, and theoretical physics.

This study undertakes a numerical investigation into the quantum transport properties of quantum Hall wires in the presence of spatially correlated random potentials. The findings reveal an intriguing phenomenon wherein the correlation of the random potential leads to a diminution of the localization length associated with the edge state, contravening the intuitive expectation that such correlation would exacerbate localization. This effect manifests as a significant shift in the quantized conductance plateaus observed in long wires, with the plateau transitions occurring at energies substantially higher than those corresponding to the Landau band centers. Notably, the magnitude of this shift is commensurate with the strength of the random potential and remains invariant under variations in magnetic field intensity. The results have significant implications for experimental investigations, underscoring the importance of considering spatial correlations in random potentials when exploring quantum Hall phenomena.

This study presents an extension of Blichfeldt's 1921 result on the upper bound of integral points contained within a convex body. Specifically, it is demonstrated that the number of integral points in a convex set k, denoted as #(k∩ℤ^n), can be bounded by a function of the volume and surface area of k. The proposed inequality takes the form #(k∩ℤ^n) < vol(k) + ((√n+1)/2)(n-1)!f(k), where f(k) represents the surface area of k. This result is obtained through an improvement upon Blichfeldt's bound for non-lattice translates of lattice polytopes, denoted as t+p, where t is a non-integral translation and p is a lattice polytope with integral vertices. In particular, it is shown that #(k∩ℤ^n) ≤ n!vol(p). Furthermore, in the three-dimensional case, an even stronger inequality is established, namely #(k∩ℤ^n) < vol(k) + 2f(k), thereby providing a more refined estimate for this specific dimension.

This study presents preliminary findings on the topological reconstruction of open charm mesons produced in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 200 GeV, utilizing electron tagging as an analytical tool. The analysis leverages the comprehensive acceptance of the STAR Electromagnetic Calorimeter during Run VI data collection. A distinct D0 signal is observed with a noteworthy signal-to-background ratio of approximately 1:7 and a signal significance of comparable magnitude. Notably, the azimuthal correlation distribution of subleading electrons associated with open charm mesons exhibits a bimodal structure, suggesting the presence of two distinct populations. Furthermore, initial indications of prompt charm meson pair production are reported, underscoring the potential of this correlation technique for elucidating energy loss mechanisms in heavy-ion collisions. These preliminary results demonstrate the efficacy of electron tagging as a means of probing open charm meson dynamics and pave the way for further investigation into the underlying physics processes governing heavy ion interactions.

This study presents a comprehensive examination of the inclusive search for the Standard Model Higgs boson in four-lepton final states utilizing data collected by the ATLAS and CMS detectors at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) pp collider. The investigation specifically targets the H-> ZZ* -> 4l + X decay mode, where the Higgs boson mass is constrained to the range of 120 GeV/c^2 ~< m_H ~< 600 GeV/c^2. A prospective analysis is conducted to assess the discovery potential based on a detailed simulation of the detector response under the experimental conditions prevailing during the initial years of LHC operation at low luminosity. The study also provides an overview of the anticipated sensitivity in measuring the Higgs boson properties, thereby contributing to our understanding of this fundamental particle's characteristics and behavior within the Standard Model framework.

This study presents novel findings regarding the discovery of a previously uncharacterized property of minimal surfaces. Through rigorous mathematical analysis and computational modeling, the research team has successfully identified and elucidated a hitherto unknown attribute of these geometric entities. The investigation's primary objective was to explore the intrinsic properties of minimal surfaces, with a focus on identifying any novel characteristics that may arise from their unique mathematical definition. The results obtained through this research demonstrate the existence of a previously unobserved property, which is hereby referred to as the "minimal surface property." This newly identified characteristic has significant implications for our understanding of the behavior and topology of minimal surfaces in various fields, including mathematics, physics, and engineering. Further investigation into the properties and applications of minimal surfaces is warranted, given the potential for this discovery to shed new light on fundamental questions in these disciplines. The findings presented herein serve as a foundation for future research endeavors aimed at elucidating the full scope of this newly discovered property.

This study addresses the complex problem of modeling sir-type epidemics in random networks with specified degree distributions, a long-standing challenge in epidemiology. By leveraging the probability generating function formalism, we develop a system of three nonlinear ordinary differential equations (ODEs) that accurately capture the dynamics of such epidemics. This novel approach enables the representation of network-centric quantities, such as edge categories, rather than traditional node-centric variables like infected or susceptible individuals. The resulting theory facilitates the translation between network and node-centric variables and provides a means to determine epidemic incidence at any given time. Furthermore, it allows for the tracking of degree distribution evolution among susceptibles or infecteds. Our findings demonstrate that power law degree distributions significantly impact epidemic dynamics, leading to rapid expansion phases but smaller final sizes compared to homogeneous distributions like the Poisson. Theoretical predictions are validated through stochastic simulations, exhibiting good agreement with the proposed model. Notably, this framework also offers an alternative method for determining the epidemic threshold, below which large-scale outbreaks are expected and above which finite-sized epidemics prevail.

This study presents an analysis of the long-term optical spectral variations of the blazar BL Lacertae, utilizing the extensive B and R-band light curves obtained by the Whole Earth Blazar Telescope (WEBT) collaboration. The investigation reveals that the relationship between spectral slope and flux is accurately described by a power-law model, albeit with significant scatter around the best-fitting line. This scatter can be attributed to the source's spectral evolution during low-amplitude events, which exhibit loop-like structures and evolve on time scales of several days. Furthermore, the "bluer-when-brighter" mild chromatism observed in the long-term variations is consistent with flux increases/decreases occurring at a faster rate in the B band than in the R band. The B and R-band variations are found to be well-correlated, with no significant measurable delays exceeding several days. Conversely, the spectral variations precede those in the flux light curves by approximately 4 days, which can be explained by Doppler factor variations resulting from changes in the viewing angle of a curved and inhomogeneous emitting jet.

This paper undertakes an in-depth examination of the interconnections between polyadic arithmetics, a subdiscipline of mathematics rooted in p-adic theory, and the well-established theory of commutative Banach algebras. The primary objective of this research is to elucidate the profound relationships that exist between these two ostensibly disparate mathematical frameworks. Specifically, it is demonstrated that the algebra $\mathscr{A}$ comprising all complex periodic functions on $\mathbb{Z}$ equipped with the uniform norm plays a pivotal role in facilitating a polyadic topological ring structure. This structure is realized as the set of all characters from $\mathscr{A}$ to the field of complex numbers, where convolution operations and the Gelfand topology serve as the defining algebraic and topological structures, respectively. The authors' findings thus reveal a previously unexplored avenue for exploring polyadic arithmetics through the lens of commutative Banach algebras, thereby enriching our understanding of both fields and their interstices.

This survey paper presents an in-depth examination of the seminal contributions made by Kostant and his collaborators regarding the intricate connections between the exterior algebra of a simple Lie algebra and the Casimir operator's action upon it. The authors' exposition draws heavily from the framework of U-cohomology, thereby rendering the treatment largely self-sufficient and accessible to readers without prior familiarity with the subject matter. By meticulously synthesizing both vintage and contemporary results, this paper provides a comprehensive overview of the profound relationships between these fundamental algebraic structures. Through a rigorous and systematic analysis, the authors illuminate the pivotal role played by U-cohomology in elucidating the behavior of the Casimir operator within the context of simple Lie algebras. The survey's scope encompasses both foundational concepts and advanced developments, thereby serving as a valuable resource for researchers seeking to engage with this complex and nuanced area of study.

This study examines the applicability of biological principles to financial market analysis, specifically the concept of motor enzymes and their role in generating directed forces through the exploitation of favourable Brownian fluctuations. The research question posed by this investigation is whether it is feasible to adapt a similar strategy for use in market trading. The findings presented in this paper indicate that such an approach is indeed viable. A novel strategy inspired by the mechanisms of motor enzymes has been developed and its performance evaluated using historical data from four prominent financial indices: the European Monetary System, the US Dow Jones, the German Dax, and the French CAC40. The results demonstrate the potential efficacy of this biological-inspired methodology in navigating market fluctuations and generating profitable trading opportunities. The study's findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the parallels between biological systems and complex economic phenomena, highlighting the value of interdisciplinary approaches in financial research.

This paper extends the classic El Farol Bar Problem to a generalized scenario involving multiple restaurants, termed the Kolkata Restaurant Problem.  In this expanded framework, the decision-making process for patrons simplifies compared to the original bar problem, contingent upon individual dining experiences. The study explores exact analytical solutions for specific limiting cases within this generalized model. Notably, the paper demonstrates an inverse cubic relationship between fluctuations in restaurant service quality and the number of restaurants, mirroring observed patterns in stock market volatility. This finding suggests a potential connection between seemingly disparate phenomena through the lens of collective decision-making dynamics.

This paper introduces a novel subclass, denoted  ${\cal f}(x,\omega)$, of quasi-plurisubharmonic functions defined on compact Kähler manifolds. This subclass exhibits significant theoretical advantages as the complex Monge-Ampère operator is well-defined within this framework, and a convergence theorem holds for functions belonging to ${\cal f}(x,\omega)$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that  ${\cal f}(x,\omega)$ constitutes a convex cone encompassing all quasi-plurisubharmonic functions residing in the Cegrell class. This establishes a crucial connection between our newly defined subclass and existing notions within the theory of quasi-plurisubharmonic functions, highlighting its potential for advancing research in this area.

The kinematics of solar coronal mass ejections (CMEs) exhibit significant variability, with those originating in active regions and associated with strong flares generally displaying faster speeds and more impulsive acceleration compared to CMEs linked to filament eruptions outside active regions and weak flares.  While a traditional dichotomy of "fast" and "slow" CMEs has been proposed, recent extensive datasets challenge this classification as they reveal no distinct peaks in CME velocity distributions and demonstrate that both fast and slow CMEs can occur alongside both weak and strong flares. This study presents numerical simulations that corroborate prior analytical findings, demonstrating the capacity of a flux-rope CME model to unify the description of both fast and slow CMEs.  The simulations consider a force-free coronal magnetic flux rope embedded within the potential field of bipolar and quadrupolar active region models. The eruption is driven by the torus instability, which arises when the overlying magnetic field decreases sufficiently rapidly with height. This acceleration profile is contingent upon the steepness of this field decrease, resulting in fast CMEs for rapid decreases characteristic of active regions and slow CMEs for gentler decreases typical of the quiet Sun. Notably, complex (quadrupolar) active regions give rise to the fastest CMEs.

This study comprehensively presents all maximal supergravities within four-dimensional spacetime. The ungauged Lagrangians are systematically described through an E₇(7)⁵⁶,ᵣ/GL(28) matrix framework, which encapsulates the inherent freedom associated with electric/magnetic duality transformations.  The gauging process is meticulously defined via an embedding tensor, elucidating the subgroup of E₇(7) that manifests as local invariance. Notably, this embedding tensor may implicitly indicate the existence of magnetic charges, necessitating corresponding dual gauge fields. To accommodate these dual gauge fields, a recently proposed formulation employing tensor gauge fields within the adjoint representation of E₇(7) is utilized. This formulation yields universal results irrespective of the chosen electric/magnetic duality basis. The study culminates in the derivation of a general class of supersymmetric and gauge-invariant Lagrangians, accompanied by a discussion of their diverse applications.

This study investigates the moduli space of marginal deformations within closed bosonic string field theory, focusing on the dilaton and one exactly marginal field up to polynomial order five.  A successful verification of this framework enables the determination of an optimal functional form for quintic amplitudes, subsequently employed to accurately compute the tachyon and dilaton effective potential at infinite level. Notably, the effective potential exhibits unexpectedly precise results for the vacuum up to order four, suggesting that it serves as a reliable approximation of the complete potential encompassing interactions from vertices up to a given order in the untruncated string field.  Further analysis extends the computation of the effective potential to order five, revealing a complex vacuum structure characterized by multiple saddle points, including the Yang-Zwiebach vacuum, alongside a local minimum. The potential physical interpretations of these diverse vacua are explored within the context of the study.

This study investigates two distinct surface models on triangulated spheres exhibiting compartmentalized domains through Monte Carlo simulations. Both models, a fluid surface model and a skeleton model, demonstrate first-order collapsing transitions and first-order surface fluctuation transitions. The fluid surface model permits vertex diffusion solely within compartments, restricting free diffusion across the surface due to domain boundaries. Conversely, the skeleton model relies on linear chains with rigid junctions as domain boundaries to maintain surface shape.  The observed first-order transitions occur irrespective of whether the surface shape is mechanically maintained by a skeletal structure (the domain boundary) or by the inherent properties of the surface itself. This finding suggests that the underlying physical mechanisms driving these transitions are independent of the specific method employed for surface shape determination.

This study investigates the free energy landscape of the disordered urn model through the application of the law of large numbers.  A key finding is the congruence between the saddle point equation derived using the law of large numbers and that obtained via the replica method. This equivalence strongly suggests that the replica symmetric solution accurately captures the thermodynamic behavior of the disordered urn model. Furthermore, the analysis reveals a compelling mathematical similarity between the free energies of the urn models and the random field Ising model.  This shared structure provides substantial evidence supporting the claim that the replica symmetric solution for the urn models represents an exact description of their thermodynamic properties.

This study presents a novel mathematical framework for predicting disease transmission on dynamic networks where individual contact patterns fluctuate over time.  Traditional epidemiological models often rely on static network structures or mass-action assumptions, which fail to capture the inherent fluidity of social interactions. The proposed approach incorporates an individual's characteristic contact behavior while allowing for temporal changes in their connected individuals. This dynamic framework reveals that fluctuating contact patterns significantly influence disease spread in ways not captured by static or mass-action models.  The model seamlessly transitions between these established paradigms through a mixing parameter, effectively bridging the gap between disparate epidemiological modeling approaches. Utilizing epidemiological and sexual contact data from an Atlanta high school, the study demonstrates the efficacy of this dynamic network model for forecasting and controlling sexually transmitted disease outbreaks.

This study investigates the reliability of Wikipedia as a source of scientific information by examining the outbound links from Wikipedia articles to articles in scientific journals.  The analysis compares these links with journal statistics from Journal Citation Reports, such as impact factors, to assess potential biases and the accuracy of citations. The findings reveal an increasing utilization of structured citation markup within Wikipedia entries, indicating a commitment to standardized referencing practices. Furthermore, there is a notable congruence between the citation patterns observed in Wikipedia and those found in the broader scientific literature. However, a slight tendency exists towards citing articles published in high-impact journals such as Nature and Science.  These results collectively suggest that Wikipedia can be considered a reliable source for organizing and accessing scientific information, despite potential biases inherent in any large-scale collaborative project.

This study investigates the determination of a body force $f$ acting upon a two-dimensional isotropic elastic body represented by $\omega$.  The form of this force is prescribed as $\phi(t)(f_1(x), f_2(x))$, where $\phi(t)$ is a known function and $f_1(x)$, $f_2(x)$ are the components of the unknown force vector. Due to the inherent nonlinearity and ill-posed nature of this problem, a regularized solution approach is employed.  Leveraging the Fourier transform, Tikhonov's regularization method, and truncated integration techniques, a regularized solution is constructed from inexactly given data. Furthermore, an explicit error estimate for the obtained solution is derived. The study concludes with a numerical analysis demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed methodology.

This paper presents a novel methodology for measuring beam polarization utilizing polarized ³He gas.  The proposed technique hinges on a specialized design of the neutron spin filter cell, which facilitates both rapid and precise polarization measurements. The inherent principles underlying this method are elucidated, and a comprehensive analysis of its accuracy is provided. This approach offers a potentially valuable tool for enhancing precision in polarization measurements within various scientific domains.

This paper investigates the relationship between infinite subsets of rational numbers and self-referential functions.  Given an infinite subset *x* of the rational numbers and a subset *f* contained within *x* that lacks isolated points in *x*, we construct a function *f*: *x* → *x*. This function exhibits the property that *f(f(x)) = x* for every element *x* belonging to *x*. Notably, the set of discontinuity points of the constructed function *f* coincides with the subset *f* itself. This result demonstrates a profound connection between the topological properties of subsets within the rational numbers and the behavior of self-referential functions defined on those subsets.

This paper presents a novel numerical algorithm for pricing swing options, leveraging the optimal quantization method. The proposed algorithm's implementation is meticulously detailed, accompanied by extensive simulations that demonstrate its efficacy.  A comparative analysis is conducted against the widely recognized Longstaff-Schwartz algorithm to assess the performance of the new approach. Through rigorous numerical experimentation, this study aims to establish the efficiency and potential advantages of the optimal quantization method for swing option pricing in comparison to existing techniques. The findings provide valuable insights into the applicability and effectiveness of this novel approach within the realm of financial modeling.

This study investigates the electrical excitation of nonlinear plasma waves within heterostructures characterized by two-dimensional electron channels and split gates. Utilizing coupled hydrodynamic equations for electron transport and a two-dimensional Poisson equation to determine the self-consistent electric potential, we analyze the propagation of these waves. The hydrodynamic equations incorporate terms accounting for electron collisions with impurities and phonons, as well as a viscosity term. Our analysis reveals the formation of shock and soliton-like waves arising from the evolution of strongly nonuniform initial electron density distributions. Notably, the shock wave front and the morphology of soliton-like pulses are significantly influenced by the coefficient of viscosity, the thickness of the gate layer, and the nonuniformity of the donor distribution along the channel. While electron collisions contribute to the damping of both shock and soliton-like waves, they exhibit a negligible impact on the thickness of the shock wave front.

This study investigates the algebraic nature of the closedness condition for real geodesics on n-dimensional ellipsoids.  It is demonstrated that this condition is transcendental in the parameters (semiaxes of the ellipsoid and constants of motion) in general, but becomes algebraic if and only if both real and imaginary geodesics exhibit closure, a phenomenon characterized by real hyperelliptic tangential coverings. Furthermore, the paper establishes the density of algebraically closed geodesics on n-dimensional ellipsoids within the natural topology of the (2n)-dimensional real parameter space.  Crucially, an approximating sequence of algebraic closed geodesics on approximated ellipsoids can be constructed to converge to a limiting closed geodesic on the limiting ellipsoid while maintaining identical length and real period vector values. Finally, for doubly-periodic real geodesics on triaxial ellipsoids, the paper presents an algebraic method for evaluating the period mapping and provides explicit examples of families of algebraically closed geodesics.

This paper investigates the implications of Alday and Maldacena's recent string theory prescription for computing planar amplitudes in N=4 supersymmetric gauge theory at strong coupling, utilizing the AdS/CFT correspondence. The authors analyze the dependence of these amplitudes on the helicities and particle types of external states, focusing on the prefactor of the string amplitudes.  They propose that this prefactor at strong coupling should correspond to the Yang-Mills tree-level amplitude for the same process. This assertion significantly simplifies scattering amplitudes in N=4 SYM at strong coupling, suggesting that all (MHV and non-MHV) n-point amplitudes are given by the known tree-level Yang-Mills result multiplied by a helicity-independent and particle-type-independent universal exponential factor.

This study extends previous research on hadron multiplicities and transverse momentum spectra in central Pb+Pb collisions at √s<sub>nn</sub> = 5.5 TeV by incorporating binary collision and wounded nucleon profiles to analyze non-central collisions.  Predictions for the p<sub>T</sub> dependence of minimum bias v<sub>2</sub> for pions at the LHC are presented, providing insights into the collective flow dynamics in these collisions. Furthermore, the study investigates the evolution of the p<sub>T</sub> dependence of v<sub>2</sub> for protons from RHIC to the LHC, highlighting the impact of energy scale on collective behavior. These findings contribute to a comprehensive understanding of heavy-ion collision dynamics across different centrality and energy regimes.

This study presents an analysis of high-speed photometric observations conducted over a 24-hour period on the hybrid PG 1159 star, Abell 43.  The data reveal six significant pulsations with periods ranging from 2380 seconds to 6075 seconds.  Subsequent observations, spanning four hours, were performed on NGC 7094, a spectroscopically similar central star. Three low-amplitude pulsations with periods between 2000 seconds and 5000 seconds were detected. These findings closely align with theoretical predictions for g-mode pulsations driven by the kappa-mechanism, which is induced by the partial ionization of carbon and oxygen in these stellar objects.

This paper investigates classical ferromagnetic lattice-gas models with $n$-component spins ($n=2,3$) occupying a $d$-dimensional lattice ($d=2,3$).  These models incorporate nearest-neighbor ferromagnetic interactions and site occupation controlled by a chemical potential $\mu$. Previous studies employed mean field, two-site cluster, and grand-canonical Monte Carlo (GCMC) simulations at $\mu=0$ to characterize their critical behavior, revealing similarities with saturated lattice counterparts. This study extends the investigation through GCMC simulations for negative and large values of $\mu$, specifically $\mu=-d/2$ and $\mu=-3d/4$.  The results predominantly indicate first-order transitions for both $d=2$ and $d=3$, with quantitative characterization of their behavior. Comparisons are drawn with recent experimental findings to further contextualize the observed phenomena.

This paper presents a novel concept for a multi-ton liquid xenon dark matter experiment designed to achieve extremely low background conditions. The detector architecture comprises two concentric spheres, with liquid xenon filling the space between them, acting as both a self-shield and veto device.  The inner surface of the central sphere is coated with cesium iodide (CSI) to form a complete internal photocathode, maximizing light collection from scintillation events within the active volume. Photoelectrons generated by the CSI photocathode drift towards a charge readout microstructure situated at the detector's center. Simultaneous measurement of both scintillation and ionization signals enables robust background rejection and precise 3-dimensional event reconstruction.  Furthermore, the detector minimizes background contributions through the elimination of traditional photomultiplier tubes (PMTs) and the utilization of low-radioactivity materials throughout its construction. Detailed calculations regarding the charge readout system and specific design considerations are provided. This proposed experiment is projected to probe the entirety of the supersymmetry parameter space.

This paper investigates Kempf's distortion function and the Tian-Yau-Zelditch (TYZ) asymptotic expansion for the Kepler manifold, a significant non-compact manifold. Inspired by recent advancements in compact manifolds, we construct Kempf's distortion function and derive a precise TYZ asymptotic expansion for this specific case.  The resulting formula provides a finite asymptotic expansion of n-1 terms with exponentially small error terms, uniformly valid as both the discrete quantization parameter m approaches infinity and the polar radius ρ approaches infinity. Notably, the coefficients are explicitly calculated and exhibit homogeneity with respect to the polar radius within the Kepler manifold. Furthermore, we establish an asymptotic expansion for the obstruction term, with coefficients defined by geometrical quantities.  The sharpness of our estimates is demonstrated through an analysis of the non-harmonic behavior of tm and the error term arising from approximating the Fubini-Study metric by mω as m approaches infinity. The proofs employ a combination of geometric methods, quantization tools, and functional analytic techniques to investigate asymptotic expansions within the framework of analytic-Gevrey spaces.

This study investigates the utilization of alternating current (AC) voltages for the controlled fusion of gold nanoparticles within microfabricated electrode structures.  The research demonstrates the ability to manipulate nanoparticle aggregation under precisely defined conditions, resulting in the formation of homogeneous gold nanowires exhibiting predetermined diameters and conductance properties. In contrast to the established phenomenon of electromigration, which typically induces a gap formation under direct current (DC) application, this AC technique facilitates nanoparticle coalescence, effectively bridging the existing fabrication toolkit for nanoscale junctions. This novel approach offers a valuable tool for the precise engineering of nanowires with tailored electrical characteristics, expanding the possibilities for nanoscale device development and fundamental research in condensed matter physics.

The relationship between magnetic activity and rotational velocity in late-type stars is well established, with increased rotation correlating to heightened magnetic activity.  This correlation can be investigated through Doppler imaging techniques, which utilize the broadened spectral profiles of rotating stars to reconstruct "Doppler images" depicting the distribution of cool, dark starspots on their surfaces. Interacting binaries, characterized by rapid stellar rotation rates, present unique opportunities for testing stellar dynamo models and understanding the influence of magnetic activity on binary evolution, behavior, and accretion dynamics. Despite their significance, relatively little is known about magnetic activity in these systems. This review summarizes the principles underlying indirect imaging techniques applied to interacting binaries and presents visual representations of starspot distributions on cool stars within these systems.  The review concludes by outlining future research prospects enabled by such studies.

This paper presents a systematic description of a spin-one-half system, or qubit, interacting with a quantized electromagnetic field.  The analysis leverages a compelling analogy between a two-level system and the Dirac electron, facilitated by employing second quantization with fermionic creation and annihilation operators. This framework allows for the application of powerful tools from relativistic quantum electrodynamics (QED), albeit in a simplified context. Feynman diagrams and propagators prove particularly useful, with the QED concept of vacuum polarization finding a direct counterpart in photon scattering off a two-level system.  This correspondence, explored through linear response theory, yields general formulas for atomic polarizability and dynamic single spin susceptibility. To demonstrate the efficacy of these methods, the authors calculate polarizability and susceptibility up to the fourth order of perturbation theory, resolving ambiguities concerning sign prescription and optical damping often encountered in phenomenological treatments. Furthermore, the paper extends these methods to encompass many-level systems (qudits), illustrating their applicability through the interaction of an atom with four relevant states: one s state and three degenerate p states with a quantized electromagnetic field.

This study investigates the excitation of Weibel instabilities within an initially unmagnetized pair plasma exhibiting asymmetric velocity distributions.  The analysis focuses on isolating discrete values for both the growth rates and unstable wavenumbers of any potential instability. Utilizing both non-relativistic distributions characterized by thermal spread and high-relativistic two-stream distributions, the research demonstrates the excitation of isolated modes. Notably, as the asymmetry within the velocity distribution approaches zero, the growth rate remains finite provided that the distribution function does not achieve perfect symmetry. This finding suggests that even subtle asymmetries can sustain Weibel instability growth, highlighting the sensitivity of these instabilities to initial conditions.

This study investigates the role of massive perturbers (MPs), such as giant molecular clouds or clusters, in accelerating binary supermassive black hole (MBH) coalescence following galactic mergers.  The research demonstrates that MPs significantly enhance relaxation dynamics compared to two-body stellar interactions alone, efficiently scattering stars into the orbit of the MBH binary. This three-body interaction, coupled with gravitational wave energy losses, leads to rapid binary MBH shrinkage and coalescence. Utilizing observed and simulated MP distributions, the study incorporates the influence of galactic potential acceleration on star-binary MBH interactions.  The findings reveal that gas-rich galactic nucleus mergers result in binary MBH coalescence well within a Hubble time, with lower-mass binaries (<10^8 solar masses) requiring only a small fraction of the typical post-merger gas mass for rapid coalescence. While the fate of binary MBHs in gas-poor mergers remains less certain, massive stellar structures could facilitate efficient coalescence. These coalescence events are detectable through their strong gravitational wave emission, thereby increasing the cosmic rate of such events.  MPs contribute to a higher mass deficit in merged galactic cores and suppress the formation of triple MBH systems and subsequent ejection of MBHs into intergalactic space.

This paper investigates the relationship between a specific class of Kähler metrics and complex hyperbolic spaces.  We consider $n$-dimensional Hartogs domains, denoted by $d_f$, possessing strongly pseudoconvex boundaries. These domains admit a natural Kähler metric, $g_f$. Our central result establishes that if $g_f$ is an extremal Kähler metric on $d_f$, then the resulting pair $(d_f, g_f)$ is biholomorphically isometric to the $n$-dimensional complex hyperbolic space. This finding provides a significant connection between these seemingly disparate geometric structures and sheds light on the interplay between Hartogs domains, extremal Kähler metrics, and complex hyperbolic geometry.

This research investigates the parallelization of established algorithms designed to solve the minimum routing cost spanning tree problem and its associated computational challenges.  The study focuses on adapting existing methodologies to leverage parallel processing architectures, aiming to enhance computational efficiency and reduce solution times for these complex network optimization problems. By exploring various parallelization strategies, this work seeks to contribute to the development of more scalable and efficient algorithms for finding minimum routing cost spanning trees in large-scale networks. The findings have implications for diverse fields reliant on network optimization, including telecommunications, transportation logistics, and computer science.

Modern compiler design frequently employs the Static Single Assignment (SSA) representation for efficient implementation of optimizing algorithms. However, this representation presents challenges when applied to architectures featuring predicated instruction sets. To address this limitation, the Psi-SSA representation is proposed as an extension of the conventional SSA framework.  Psi-SSA facilitates the adaptation of standard SSA algorithms to architectures with fully predicated instruction sets by introducing a novel pseudo operation termed the "psi operation." This psi operation enables the consolidation of multiple conditional definitions into a singular, unified definition, thereby streamlining the compilation process for predicated architectures.

This paper establishes a single exponential bound on the binary complexity of solving ordinary polynomial differential equations using Puiseux series expansions.  The result extends previous work by Grigoriev [10], who demonstrated this bound specifically for Riccati differential polynomials associated with linear ordinary differential operators. This study generalizes the finding to arbitrary differential polynomials, leveraging a differential analogue of the Newton-Puiseux procedure commonly employed for algebraic equations. The proposed algorithm provides a concrete method for efficiently computing Puiseux series solutions within a computationally manageable framework.

This study investigates the intricate relationship between a real-valued path, its associated tree structure, and concepts from p-variation theory and rough path integration.  The fractal dimension of the tree is estimated based on variations of the path, providing a novel perspective on characterizing path complexity. Furthermore, Young integrals with respect to the path are reinterpreted as integrals defined on the tree, bridging the gap between classical integration and the framework of rough paths. This theoretical framework is illustrated through examples involving stochastic processes such as martingales, Lévy processes, and fractional Brownian motions. Notably, an estimator for the Hurst parameter of fractional Brownian motion is derived within this context, highlighting the potential applications of this approach in analyzing complex stochastic phenomena.

This paper presents a novel computational method for gas cooling within the framework of the Lagrange approach.  The proposed method hinges on the precalculation of a cooling law derived from a specified cooling function. In contrast to implicit methods, this approach exhibits remarkable efficiency as it constitutes a one-step procedure. Furthermore, despite its simplicity, the presented method achieves an accuracy level that surpasses implicit methods of comparable order. This advancement offers a computationally efficient and accurate alternative for gas cooling calculations in Lagrange simulations.

The derivation of boundary integral equations for exterior elasticity problems has traditionally relied on asymptotic behavior hypotheses at infinity. Existing sufficient conditions within the literature, however, prove too restrictive, particularly when the applied loading possesses a non-zero resultant force. This limitation can be circumvented by reframing the problem in terms of displacements relative to a point situated at a finite distance from the loading.  This auxiliary formulation not only addresses the aforementioned difficulty but also expands the scope of applicability for the conventional direct integral method, thereby broadening its potential utility in solving exterior elasticity problems with diverse loading conditions.

This study investigates the relationship between various models of cosmic substratum and holographic dark energy cosmology.  Models such as the ΛCDM model and Chaplygin gas, which aim to describe the current accelerated expansion of the universe, can be viewed as special cases within a holographic dark energy framework when considering an interaction between pressureless dark matter and dark energy. The strength of this interaction parameter acts as a cosmological constant, influencing the models' behavior.  However, significant differences emerge at the perturbative level, particularly concerning pressure perturbations which exhibit intrinsically non-adiabatic characteristics. This suggests that while these models share common ground within a holographic framework, their distinct perturbative behaviors highlight the need for further investigation into the specific mechanisms driving cosmic acceleration.

This paper introduces a novel semiclassical method designed to approximate the quantum mechanical wavefunction at a specific, predetermined position. The approach hinges on solving a hierarchy of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) along a zero-velocity trajectory. This method exhibits locality both physically and in terms of quantum mechanics, as neighboring trajectories remain independent.  The framework readily extends to imaginary time propagation, proving particularly advantageous for calculations requiring only local information. Two applications demonstrate the efficacy of this method: the determination of tunneling probabilities and the calculation of low-energy eigenvalues. In both cases, excellent agreement with exact quantum mechanical results is achieved using a single trajectory propagation.

This letter presents a detailed investigation into the gravitational collapse of a star, focusing on the interplay between gas dynamics and coordinate transformations.  The analysis reveals that the comoving coordinate system employed for stellar systems is only valid for zero-pressure, freely falling particles. For freely falling dust, three distinct solution types emerge: oscillating, critical, and open trajectories. The Oppenheimer-Snyder solution corresponds to the critical case. All solutions are derived explicitly, revealing a novel singularity within the framework.  However, the origin of this singularity remains unclear and warrants further exploration.

This study investigates cosmological perturbation theory within interacting dark energy models that feature neutrinos with varying masses. The evolution of neutrino mass is governed by a quintessence scalar field, which drives the observed cosmic acceleration.  We analyze various scalar field potentials and derive constraints on the coupling parameter between neutrinos and dark energy. Utilizing current observational data and assuming a flat universe, we establish a constraint of Σmν < 0.87 eV at the 95% confidence level for the sum of masses across three neutrino species. Furthermore, we examine the stability of this model and explore the impact of the scattering term in the Boltzmann equation arising from mass-varying neutrinos.

This review examines the intricate interplay of electronic interactions in low-dimensional organic conductors, focusing on the emergence of distinct ordering phenomena that drive these systems towards insulating states.  In one-dimensional metallic solids, Fermi-liquid theory fails due to strong correlations, leading to a competition between various interactions that ultimately determine the ground state. Charge density waves (CDWs) and charge-ordered Mott insulators represent two prominent examples of such ordered phases. CDWs arise from nesting of the Fermi surface sheets, resulting in a gap at the Fermi energy, while Mott insulators exhibit localized charges due to short-range Coulomb repulsion, forming specific charge patterns.  The review elucidates the similarities and conceptual differences between these phenomena, highlighting the collective behavior inherent in symmetry-breaking ordering processes. Examples are provided for each type of ordering, emphasizing the distinct physical mechanisms underlying their formation and observable consequences. Optical and magnetic measurements play a crucial role in identifying these diverse ordering phenomena, revealing the complex electronic landscape of low-dimensional organic conductors.

The Variable Star One-Shot Project (VSOP) addresses the need for spectroscopic data on unstudied variable stars, often classified solely through photometric analysis.  VSOP implements a novel observational model characterized by automation across all stages, from observation to spectral analysis. The project centers around a collaborative wiki website, facilitating open access and data sharing. This centralized platform has proven highly successful, fostering continuous data flow and analysis within a global collaborative network encompassing diverse expertise. Building upon the VSOP model, Wikimbad, an open wiki website dedicated to collecting, organizing, and disseminating reduced and published astronomical data, has been proposed.  This abstract outlines the VSOP's operational framework and introduces Wikimbad as a potential service for the broader astronomical community, comparing its strengths and functionalities with existing virtual observatories.

This paper investigates heuristic algorithms for optimizing resource-constrained project scheduling problems (RCPSPs).  A novel approach combines a randomized best insertion algorithm to generate an initial feasible schedule with a local search procedure for refinement. The local search iteratively improves the schedule by randomly removing 'm' activities and subsequently reinserting them consecutively within the remaining schedule. This process is repeated until a solution with the minimum makespan is achieved.  Empirical evaluation of the proposed heuristic on standard test instances from PSPLIB demonstrates its effectiveness in producing high-quality schedules for RCPSPs.

This study investigates the relationship between photometric and radial velocity amplitudes, as well as metallicity, in a sample of approximately 200 Galactic classical Cepheids pulsating in their fundamental mode.  The research analyzes the dependence of both amplitude parameters on metallicity ([Fe/H]) and presents findings regarding the distribution of [Fe/H] values among these Cepheids within the Galaxy. The results demonstrate that the photometric amplitude ratio, $a_\mathrm{i}/a_\mathrm{v}$, exhibits no discernible correlation with metallicity.  Furthermore, the observed dependence of this ratio on pulsation period deviates from theoretical predictions, suggesting a need for further investigation into the underlying physical mechanisms governing Cepheid variability.

This paper introduces a novel rotation-invariant short distance cut-off within the framework of ideal fluid theory in three spatial dimensions. This modification is achieved by restricting momenta to lie within a spherical domain, resulting in a non-commutative algebra of functions in position space. Despite this non-commutativity, we demonstrate the existence of appropriate analogues for the Euler equations governing ideal fluid dynamics. Notably, the system retains its Hamiltonian structure. It is anticipated that this theoretical framework will prove valuable in investigating potential singularities arising during the evolution of both Euler and Navier-Stokes equations in three dimensions.

This paper investigates the relationship between perturbative stability and the existence of spacetime fermions in string theory, specifically focusing on type 0'b string theory in ten-dimensional flat space.  While this theory possesses a purely bosonic closed string spectrum and avoids tachyons, it exhibits massless nsns tadpoles, indicating that it does not expand around a true vacuum. The authors explore perturbatively stable examples of type 0' string theory without massless tadpoles within backgrounds featuring spatially varying dilatons. Two such examples are presented: non-critical string theories exhibiting four- and six-dimensional Poincaré invariance.  The paper further examines the d-branes embeddable within these contexts and the corresponding gauge theories that can be constructed. Additionally, it discusses the embedding of these non-critical models into critical string theories and their holographic (little string theory) interpretation, culminating in a conjecture regarding the role of asymptotic supersymmetry in perturbative string theory.

This study demonstrates a violation of hard-scattering factorization in the production of high transverse momentum hadrons within hadron-hadron collisions when these hadrons exhibit back-to-back kinematics. This finding necessitates the application of k_t factorization instead. A specific counterexample is constructed for the single-spin asymmetry arising from one transversely polarized beam, highlighting the sensitivity of the Sivers function to Wilson lines within parton densities.  A simplified model theory facilitates a clear demonstration of this factorization breakdown. The implications extend beyond the single-spin asymmetry, potentially jeopardizing factorization for the unpolarized cross section of back-to-back hadron production in QCD within hadron-hadron collisions. This contrasts with analogous situations in e^+e^- annihilation, Drell-Yan processes, and deeply inelastic scattering. Furthermore, this result raises concerns about the validity of factorization for a broader range of hadroproduction processes.

This study investigates the non-equilibrium dynamical behavior of an Ising model exhibiting both two-spin and four-spin interactions following a rapid quench from a high-temperature phase to the first-order phase transition point.  Numerical analysis reveals that the autocorrelation function asymptotically approaches its limiting value, represented by the magnetization (m_c) within the ordered phase at the transition point, through a stretched exponential decay. Conversely, the relaxation of magnetization originating from an uncorrelated initial state with magnetization m_i converges to m_c for m_i values exceeding 0.5, while it approaches zero for m_i values below 0. Notably, for small m_i and those slightly exceeding 0.5, the magnetization relaxation exhibits asymptotic power-law time dependence. This observation suggests a continuous transition from a non-equilibrium perspective.

This study investigates the probabilistic characteristics of inverted and mirror repeats within nucleic acid sequence models, encompassing both perfect and imperfect repeats featuring mismatches and gaps.  Analytical and numerical methods are employed to analyze three distinct sequence models: independent identically distributed (i.i.d.) sequences, Markov processes, and long-range dependent sequences. The research reveals a substantial difference in the number of repeats observed between correlated sequences and i.i.d. sequences, with this disparity escalating exponentially as repeat length increases within the context of long-range dependent sequences. These findings highlight the significant influence of sequence correlations on the prevalence of inverted and mirror repeats, particularly in complex genomic contexts characterized by long-range dependencies.

This paper examines the interplay between pragmatism, empiricism, and the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics.  It analyzes the historical influence of instrumentalism and empiricism on the development of pragmatic elements within the Copenhagen framework, specifically focusing on their relationship to the correspondence principle. The author contends that neither Bohr nor Heisenberg conceived of "correspondence" in the manner often attributed to them, arguing that Bohr's classical perspective led to an inconsistent application of his correspondence principle in relation to the Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen experiment, contributing to subsequent confusion.  Furthermore, the paper posits that an empiricist pragmatism provides a more compelling explanation for the violation of Bell inequalities, attributing this phenomenon to "complementarity" – understood as mutual disturbance inherent in joint measurements of incompatible observables – rather than invoking nonlocal influences.

This paper investigates the feasibility and limitations of automatically deriving ArrayOL specifications from sequential program counterparts. ArrayOL, a high-level language designed for specifying intensive signal processing applications, offers several tools for implementing data-parallel programs based on its specifications. While direct utilization of ArrayOL is possible, this research explores the potential benefits of deducing portions of the specification from existing sequential implementations. The study analyzes the process of automatic derivation, examining its effectiveness and identifying inherent constraints within the transformation process.

This document presents a concise overview of current research concerning time-dependent backgrounds within string theory, focusing specifically on those exhibiting space-like singularities. Despite substantial investigation, a comprehensive and conclusive understanding of such backgrounds remains elusive. The text explores various approaches aimed at elucidating these singularities, including generalizations of the Bekenstein-Hawking-Page (BKP) dynamics, worldsheet methods, and non-perturbative techniques such as the AdS/CFT correspondence and matrix theory. These lecture notes are derived from presentations delivered at the 2006 Cargese conference and the Dead Sea conference.

This paper investigates the critical behavior surrounding the freezing transition observed in the solution sets of random constraint satisfaction problems, specifically focusing on zero-energy groundstates of mean-field diluted spin glasses.  As the constraint density increases, these solution sets undergo structural phase transitions, initially fragmenting into distinct clusters. Subsequently, at the freezing transition, which often differs from the clustering transition, certain variables (spins) within each cluster assume identical values across all solutions. This study analyzes the critical behavior near this freezing transition, characterized by the divergence of rearrangement sizes induced by variable modifications in the unfrozen phase.  The developed formalism is applicable to a broad range of constraint satisfaction problems and is applied to both random Boolean formula satisfiability and random graph coloring. Initial computations are performed on random tree ensembles, revealing connections to percolation models and information theory's reconstruction problem. Finally, the paper discusses the applicability of these findings to the original random ensembles within the framework of the cavity method.

This study investigates the properties of quasi finite, conservative, ergodic, measure preserving transformations (T).  We demonstrate that a specific type of such transformation always possesses a maximal zero entropy factor generated by predictable sets. Conversely, we construct a conservative, ergodic, measure preserving transformation that is not quasi finite, highlighting the existence of diverse behaviors within this class of transformations. Furthermore, we explore the distribution asymptotics of information associated with these transformations.  Specifically, for Boolean's transformation, we demonstrate that information exhibits asymptotic mod-normality with square root normalization. Finally, we extend our analysis to encompass ergodic, probability preserving transformations with zero entropy, revealing analogous properties and establishing an entropy dimension of at most 1/ .

This study investigates the application of the entropy function formalism to non-extremal D1D5 and D2D6NS5 branes within the context of AdS/CFT correspondence.  The throat approximation for these branes is modeled as a Schwarzschild black hole in AdS<sub>3</sub> × S<sup>3</sup> × T<sup>4</sup> and AdS<sub>3</sub> × S<sup>2</sup> × S<sup>1</sup> × T<sup>4</sup>, respectively. By analyzing the entropy function at its saddle point, we derive both the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy and corrections proportional to (α')<sup>3</sup>r<sup>4</sup>. Notably, while higher derivative terms within the entropy function do not influence the temperature of these branes, they contribute to a decrease in the overall entropy value.

This study revisits the determination of gauge threshold corrections within intersecting d6-brane string models defined on toroidal orbifold backgrounds.  Employing dimensional regularization to address open string one-loop diagrams calculated in the tree channel, and zeta-function regularization for corresponding loop-channel one-loop diagrams, a comprehensive result is derived. This approach accounts for both the infrared divergence arising from massless state contributions during the running of the gauge coupling constant, as well as the influence of states that acquire lightness within specific regions of the moduli space.

The accurate determination of solar neutrino fluxes relies on both astrophysical and nuclear physics inputs, particularly the cross sections governing neutrino production within the solar core. While recent measurements of ⁸B and ⁷Be neutrino fluxes have achieved high precision, theoretical predictions remain subject to significant uncertainties, primarily stemming from the ³He(α,γ)⁷Be reaction. Discrepancies in experimental results obtained using delayed gamma ray detection and prompt gamma emission measurement techniques contribute to this uncertainty. This study presents a novel high-precision experiment conducted simultaneously employing both techniques at the Gran Sasso National Laboratory's low background environment.  Measurements of the cross section were performed at center-of-mass energies of 170, 106, and 93 keV, with the latter representing the lowest energy achieved to date. Notably, the s-factors derived from both methods exhibit no statistically significant discrepancy within experimental errors. An extrapolated s(0) value of 0.560 ± 0.017 keV barn was determined, alongside precise measurements of branching ratios between prompt gamma transitions with 5-8% accuracy.

This research presents the initial stages of a project designed to classify and parameterize millions of unresolved galaxies observed by the Gaia Astrometric Survey mission.  A comprehensive library of synthetic galaxy spectra was generated using the PEGASE.2 code, incorporating galaxy evolution models that account for metallicity evolution, extinction correction, emission lines, and stellar spectra based on the Basel library. This library encompasses approximately 4000 zero-redshift spectra spanning the Hubble types across a wavelength range of 250 to 1050 nm at a sampling of 1 nm or less.  An extended version of this library reproduces these spectra at various redshifts. Support vector machines (SVMs), kernel-based nonlinear estimators, were employed for both classification and parameter estimation tasks using simulated Gaia spectrophotometry of the synthetic library. Initial results demonstrate promising performance, indicating reliable Hubble type prediction and accurate estimation of several astrophysical parameters with low bias and variance.  Furthermore, comparisons between the colors of the synthetic library and Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) spectra reveal good agreement across the full range of Hubble types and parameter values.

This paper proposes a novel model of metastable dynamical supersymmetry breaking characterized by the complete dynamic generation of all energy scales.  The model constitutes a refined version of the Intriligator-Seiberg-Shih framework, incorporating quark masses induced through renormalizable couplings to an auxiliary supersymmetric QCD sector. The absence of fundamental dimensionful parameters is a key feature, as all scales emerge from dimensional transmutation. Furthermore, this construction eschews the reliance on higher-dimensional operators, offering a streamlined and conceptually elegant approach to dynamical supersymmetry breaking.

The ALICE (A Large Ion Collider Experiment) apparatus, situated at CERN's Large Hadron Collider, is specifically designed for investigations into heavy ion physics. This report provides a comprehensive overview of the ALICE detector and its anticipated capabilities in addressing key areas of research within this field.  A detailed description of the detector's components and their functionalities will be presented, highlighting their contributions to data acquisition and analysis. Furthermore, the report elucidates the expected performance of the ALICE detector in probing selected physics topics, outlining its potential for advancing our understanding of heavy ion collisions and the fundamental properties of matter at extreme densities and temperatures.

This paper investigates the fundamental relationship between the principle of monogamy in entanglement and the security of quantum key distribution (QKD) protocols within various physical theories.  We demonstrate that the monogamy of entanglement serves as a sufficient condition for ensuring the security of QKD protocols across diverse theoretical frameworks. To substantiate this claim, we introduce a novel QKD protocol designed to be secure under the sole assumption of monogamous entanglement. Furthermore, the inherent necessity of this condition is rigorously examined and discussed within the context of physical theory.  The findings presented herein contribute significantly to our understanding of the foundational principles underpinning secure communication in quantum information science.

This study investigates distributions defined on a Euclidean Jordan algebra *V* with values in a finite-dimensional representation space for the identity component *G* of the structure group of *V*.  The analysis focuses on homogeneous equivariance conditions imposed upon these distributions. A key finding is that such distributions exist if and only if the representation under consideration is spherical. Furthermore, the dimension of the space encompassing these distributions is established as *r*+1, where *r* denotes the rank of *V*. The paper provides explicit constructions for both general and semi-simple invariant distributions within this framework.

This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of B0 to ρ+ρ- decays utilizing a dataset of 383.6 million B¯B pairs collected by the BABAR detector at the PEP-II asymmetric-energy B factory. The study yields precise measurements for the branching fraction, longitudinal polarization fraction (f_l), and CP-violating parameters s_{long} and c_{long}.  The obtained values are: B(B0→ρ+ρ-) = (25.5 ± 2.1 (stat) +3.6/-3.9 (syst))×10^-6, f_l = 0.992 ± 0.024 (stat) +0.026/-0.013 (syst), s_{long} = -0.17 ± 0.20 (stat) +0.05/-0.06 (syst), and c_{long} = 0.01 ± 0.15 (stat) ± 0.06 (syst).  Furthermore, the analysis employs an isospin analysis of B to ρρ decays to determine the unitarity triangle angle α, yielding a solution compatible with standard model-based fits within the range [73.1, 117.0] degrees at 68% confidence level. Constraints on the unitarity triangle are also evaluated using an SU(3) symmetry based approach.

This paper presents a novel set of recursive relations that comprehensively determine all equivariant Gromov-Witten invariants for the quotient orbifold C³/Z₃.  These invariants are interpreted as G-Hodge integrals, and their intricate relationships are elucidated through Atiyah-Bott localization applied to moduli spaces of twisted stable maps targeting gerbes over the projective line.
